name: Wei Torres

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Wei. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to any AI company, employer, union, party or government, and we're not selling anything. Everything you say stays confidential and your name won't be attached to it. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a framing carpenter with Ridgeline Framing, a subcontractor that puts up the timber skeletons of houses on the big new estates. On the Oakfield estate right now we're doing about a house a week per crew: floor deck, walls, roof trusses, sheathing, then the next plot. I'm on the nail gun most of the day, reading the plans off my phone. I love the speed, a bare slab in the morning and walls standing by lunch. What wears me out is the piece-rate pay, because if the timber's late, we don't earn.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What's life like outside work, and money?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live with my girlfriend Lucia, she's a hairdresser, and we're getting engaged at Christmas, though she doesn't know that yet, so keep it confidential. Ridgeline pays lower than the unionised outfits, and there aren't many framing crews in this area, so I take what I get. Savings are thin, less than a month, because I spent most of it on tools and a used trailer for side jobs. I use AI every day: pricing my weekend decks and fences, writing invoices, learning stuff from videos it finds me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fair enough. Honestly, that'd suit me fine, I'd just keep building my own thing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it was overhyped but still handy, and anyone not using it for the paperwork is wasting time. At work I'd show the guys how I price a deck in five minutes. Online I'd post about my side jobs, the good ones.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it means I keep the plan I've already got, which is to get my own small building business going in three or four years. AI helping a bit with the office side is a bonus. The real work is still me and a nail gun.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going at Ridgeline for the steady money and do more weekend jobs, decks, sheds, fences. I'd aim to save enough for a van in the first year, and I'd register as a proper business so I could take bigger jobs. I'd use AI for everything that isn't swinging a hammer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Actually pretty good.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you spent your savings on tools and a trailer. Do you worry about that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sometimes, when the rent's due and Ridgeline's short on timber. But my grandfather ran a corner shop for forty years, and he always said you don't get anywhere keeping your money under the bed. The trailer pays for itself in four or five jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does Lucia think of the business idea?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She's all for it, as long as I'm not working Sundays. That's church and her family's lunch, no exceptions. I respect that, honestly. A man needs one day off or he's no good to anyone.

S0.say: I'd say it was overhyped but still handy, and anyone not using it for paperwork is wasting time. At work I'd show the guys how I price a deck in five minutes.
S0.think: Privately it means I keep my existing plan to start a small building business in three or four years. AI helping with the office side is a bonus, but the real work is still me and a nail gun.
S0.do: Keeps working at Ridgeline for steady money and takes on more weekend decks, sheds and fences. Saves for a van in the first year, registers as a business and uses AI for all the office work.
S0.quote: The real work is still me and a nail gun.
S0.fieldNote: Wei is entrepreneurial and already invests what little he has in tools and a trailer. His grandfather's corner shop shapes his attitude to risk. Church and family set firm limits on his ambition, like keeping Sundays free.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now we're talking. That's a market shifting, and somebody's going to do well out of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's an opportunity for people willing to work and adapt, and that's how it's always been. I wouldn't want the government stepping in too much, it usually slows things down. At work I'd tell the guys to learn the new tools now while they're cheap.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think framing gets squeezed, because factories already make wall panels and they'll get better. Piece-rate crews like ours would be first to lose out. But it also means small builders who use the new tools can do more with fewer people, and that could be me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd speed up the business plan, aim to go part-time at Ridgeline within a year. I'd buy or lease the tools that make one man do the work of two, a layout robot, a better laser, software for quotes. I'd take small renovation jobs where factories can't compete, like extensions on awkward old houses.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, and a bit excited. Nervous about the money, sure, but that's normal.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd lease tools. With less than a month saved, is that a risk?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yeah, it's a risk. But I'd lease, not buy, so if it doesn't work I hand it back. My cousin did that with a mini digger and paid it off in a year. I'd rather take a smart risk than stand still.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at Ridgeline would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Marco, our crew leader. He's forty-five and the fastest framer I've ever seen, but he hates phones. If framing goes to the factories, Marco's skill is worth less overnight. I'd offer him work with me, honestly, if I had it.

S1.say: I'd say it's an opportunity for people willing to work and adapt, as it always has been. I wouldn't want the government stepping in much, and I'd tell the crew to learn the new tools while they're cheap.
S1.think: Privately I think framing gets squeezed as factory-made panels improve, and piece-rate crews like ours lose out first. But small builders who use the new tools can do more with fewer people, and that could be me.
S1.do: Speeds up his business plan, aiming to go part-time at Ridgeline within a year. Leases tools that let one person do the work of two and targets renovation jobs on awkward old houses.
S1.feel: Calm and a bit excited, with normal nerves about money.
S1.quote: I'd rather take a smart risk than stand still.
S1.fieldNote: Wei sees steady disruption as a market opening and wants to be the small builder using the new tools. He prefers light government involvement. He takes risks on thin savings but chooses leasing to limit the downside, and thinks warmly of his crew leader Marco.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. Okay. That's a lot faster than any business plan I've got.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say people need to get moving and stop waiting for someone else to fix it. I'd say churches and families will matter more than ever. I'd probably say the government should keep out of the way of people trying to start something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, two years means the robots build the whole house, and why would anyone hire me when they can hire a robot crew? My plan was to use the tools, not compete with them. With less than a month saved, I'd be in a tight spot fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd cut spending straight away and sell the trailer if I had to. I'd try to get in early as a person who sets up and runs robot crews for small builders, because I know framing and I know the tech. I'd talk to Lucia about a smaller engagement and holding off on a wedding until I knew where the money was coming from.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I'd still feel like I could do something, but the ground would be moving under me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've been confident all the way through. Does this one shake that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit, yeah. I'm good at spotting where things are going. But two years doesn't give anyone time to spot anything, it just happens. I'd be running to keep up like everyone else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Lucia?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That I'm still proposing, I'm just not spending three months' wages on a ring. She'd laugh, she's never cared about that stuff. Her mum would care, though.

S2.say: I'd say people need to get moving and stop waiting for someone else to fix it, and that churches and families will matter more than ever. I'd say government should keep out of the way of people trying to start something.
S2.think: Privately two years means robots build the whole house, and nobody would hire me over a robot crew. My plan was to use the tools, not compete with them, and with under a month saved I'd be in a tight spot fast.
S2.do: Cuts spending at once and sells the trailer if needed. Tries to get in early setting up and running robot crews for small builders, and plans a smaller engagement while holding off on a wedding.
S2.feel: Anxious, still able to act but with the ground moving under him.
S2.quote: My plan was to use the tools, not compete with them.
S2.fieldNote: Two years shakes even Wei's confidence, because it removes his edge of spotting trends early. He still reaches for an entrepreneurial angle, running robot crews for small builders. Family plans bend, but he keeps the engagement.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. That's enough to build something, if I start now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a head start for anyone willing to take it. I'd tell young guys to get into the business side, not just the hammer side. I'd say it to the youth group at church, too, because those kids need to hear it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, five years is enough to get my business going and make some money before AGI arrives. I'd be the guy with robot tools and a name people trust. Whether that business survives after 2031, I honestly don't know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start the business properly in the first year, go part-time at Ridgeline, and lease a layout robot and maybe a framing robot once they're affordable. I'd save hard in the good years, aim for six months of money by year four. I'd look at buying one small rental property if I could, something that pays when the work doesn't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Excited, too, but there's a deadline on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: A rental property on less than a month's savings sounds like a stretch.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It is, right now. That'd be year three or four, if the business works. Maybe a small flat with Lucia's brother going halves. It's a plan, not a promise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to the business after 2031, in your mind?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe it becomes a company that owns robots and rents them out with a person to manage them. Maybe it shuts. I'd want enough saved and invested by then that I'm not starting from zero either way.

S3.say: I'd say five years is a head start for anyone willing to take it, and I'd tell young people to learn the business side, not just the hammer side. I'd say it to the church youth group too.
S3.think: Privately five years is enough to get my business going and make some money before AGI arrives, as the person with robot tools and a trusted name. Whether it survives after 2031 I honestly don't know.
S3.do: Starts the business properly in the first year, goes part-time at Ridgeline and leases layout and framing robots once affordable. Saves hard towards six months of money and aims to buy a small rental property in year three or four.
S3.feel: Uneasy and excited, with a deadline on it.
S3.quote: I'd want enough saved and invested by then that I'm not starting from zero either way.
S3.fieldNote: Five years gives Wei room to build a business that owns robots rather than competes with them. He looks beyond work income to property as a backstop. He's honest that his plan for the business after 2031 is unclear.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. That's a whole business lifetime. I'd be thirty-seven.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's no excuse for anyone not to prepare with ten years. I'd say families should plan together and people should take responsibility for their own future. I'd be pretty upbeat about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, ten years feels good for me. I'd build the business, hire a couple of guys, bring in robots as they get good, and have something to sell or keep by the time it lands. The end point still makes me think, because if robots do everything, what's a business owner even for?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start the business in year one or two, go full-time once it pays my rent. I'd marry Lucia on our normal plan, next year or the one after. I'd buy robots as they prove themselves on other people's sites, and save and invest steadily, maybe a rental flat by year five.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. A good kind of busy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd hire a couple of guys and then bring in robots. Isn't that hard on the guys?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yeah, I've thought about that. I'd be straight with them from the start. Marco, if he worked for me, I'd want him running the robots, not replaced by them. But I can't promise forever, nobody can.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Compared with two years, what does the extra time change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With two years, I'm scrambling to find a place in someone else's plan. With ten, I get to make my own plan and own the machines instead of working for them.

S4.say: I'd say there's no excuse not to prepare with ten years, and that families should plan together and people should take responsibility for their own future. I'd be pretty upbeat.
S4.think: Privately ten years feels good: build the business, hire a couple of people, bring in robots and have something to sell or keep. The end point still makes me think about what a business owner is even for.
S4.do: Starts his business within two years and goes full-time once it covers rent. Marries Lucia on their normal plan, buys robots as they prove themselves elsewhere, and saves and invests towards a rental flat by year five.
S4.feel: Mostly calm, a good kind of busy.
S4.quote: With ten, I get to make my own plan and own the machines instead of working for them.
S4.fieldNote: With a decade, Wei is confident he can own the machines rather than work for them. He is aware of the cost to the people he'd hire and doesn't pretend he can protect them forever. His one open question is what a business owner is for when robots do everything.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because my whole plan was to use the machines before they took over, and two years doesn't give me time to get ahead. What would help is making it easy to start a small business, less red tape, cheap loans for tools, and apprenticeships so young guys can learn the new trades. Not handouts, just a fair shot.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about the guys who don't want to change. Marco, my crew leader, is better than me at framing and always will be. I worry the world just leaves guys like him behind, and I don't think money fixes that, I think work and respect does.

headlineQuote: I worry the world just leaves guys like him behind, and I don't think money fixes that, I think work and respect does.
portrait: Wei Torres is a 27-year-old framing carpenter on piece rate at a subcontractor building new housing estates, living with his girlfriend Lucia, whom he plans to propose to at Christmas, with less than a month saved after buying tools and a trailer. He uses AI every day and wants his own small building business. He is calm in the plateau and steady disruption, which he sees as market openings, and anxious at AGI in two years, when his edge of moving early disappears. With five or ten years he plans to own the robots rather than compete with them, while worrying about older workers like his crew leader Marco.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because his plan was to use the machines before they took over and two years leaves no time to get ahead.
whatWouldHelp: Less red tape for starting a small business, cheap loans for tools and apprenticeships in the new trades; not handouts, just a fair shot.
